A New UN Resolution Takes a Step Toward Decolonizing World Maps

A geography professor argues that the UN's "Correct the Map" resolution is a meaningful step toward decolonizing cartography, but notes that online platforms like Google Maps still use the Web Mercator projection, limiting the resolution's practical impact on everyday mapping.

Key takeaways
  • The UN resolution (A/RES/80/297) was adopted 164-1 with 6 abstentions; the US was the sole opponent
  • The Mercator projection's distortions were known for centuries but only politically challenged in the 1970s, beginning with Arno Peters' equal-area map
  • The Equal Earth projection (2018) is positioned as a less controversial alternative to the Gall-Peters projection
  • Web Mercator remains the default for Google Maps and similar platforms, perpetuating the same distortions the UN resolution seeks to correct
  • Online maps don't just reproduce Mercator's size distortions — they also structure worldviews around road networks, business accessibility, and consumption
  • Maps are "instruments of power" that influence how we see and interact with the world, not neutral representations
2026-09-11 Sébastien Caquard (The Tyee / The Conversation) Source article

After Google Maps, Simon Weckert Now Targets AI Cameras With "Digital Camouflage" Shirt

Six years after tricking Google Maps with 99 smartphones to fake a Berlin traffic jam, artist Simon Weckert has created a "Digital Camouflage" shirt that uses adversarial patterns to make its wearer invisible to AI-powered surveillance cameras.

Key takeaways
  • Weckert's "Digital Camouflage" shirt uses psychedelic patterns designed to defeat YOLO object detection algorithms
  • The technique uses "adversarial attacks" — the pattern is iteratively modified until the algorithm's confidence in detecting a person drops below threshold
  • The project is a response to 30 new AI-assisted surveillance cameras installed at Kottbusser Tor in Berlin's Kreuzberg district
  • The cameras are not yet active; their activation is expected after Berlin's September 20 election
  • Weckert's 2020 "Google Maps hack" used 99 smartphones in a cart to create a fake traffic jam on Google Maps in Berlin
  • The new project shifts from manipulating cartographic data to exposing the fragility of AI vision systems

"Correct the Map" Resolution: From Cartographic Question to Cultural and Political Issue

In an interview with Africa Radio, Speak Up Africa co-founder Fara Ndiaye discusses the UN's adoption of the "Correct the Map" resolution, arguing that cartographic representation is not merely a technical issue but a cultural and political one that shapes how generations perceive the world.

Key takeaways
  • The "Correct the Map" campaign was launched by NGOs Africa No Filter and Speak Up Africa, co-founded by Fara Ndiaye
  • The campaign does not exclusively promote Equal Earth — it advocates ending the default use of Mercator, and would accept any equal-area projection
  • Equal Earth was chosen partly because it is free to use and less controversial than the Gall-Peters projection
  • 164 countries voted in favor — described as "not Africa against Western countries, but 164 countries against one"
  • The campaign's next phase focuses on working with education ministries to update school textbooks
  • The resolution also calls on UN agencies to update their working documents to use equal-area projections as the default
  • Ndiaye emphasizes the issue affects not just Africa but also Latin America and South Asia, whose surfaces are particularly reduced on Mercator

Mapping Silicate Minerals From Space

NASA-funded scientists have created the first global maps of silicate, sulfate, and carbonate minerals in Earth's arid regions using thermal infrared spectroscopy data from the ECOSTRESS and ASTER satellite sensors, enabling space-based identification of mineral resources including lithium-bearing rocks.

Key takeaways
  • Researchers created 1-kilometer resolution global maps of silicate, sulfate, and carbonate minerals using ECOSTRESS (ISS) and ASTER (Terra satellite) thermal infrared data
  • Thermal infrared spectroscopy is the only known method to detect silica from space, using each mineral's unique spectral signature
  • Silicate deposits are associated with lithium-bearing minerals used in batteries, making the maps valuable for resource exploration
  • Silicate alteration on the surface can also indicate underground geothermal activity, pointing to potential renewable energy sites
  • The maps were validated by comparing satellite observations with field data from sites in California, New Mexico, and Morocco
  • The data complement NASA's EMIT sensor, which detects oxides, sulfides, and clays associated with precious minerals
  • The dataset is publicly available through NASA's Earthdata Search and the Land Processes DAAC as GeoTIFF
2026-09-11 Charlie Plain (NASA Earthdata) Source article

Correcting the Map, as We Must, and Yet Still

A legal scholar analyzes the UN's "Correct the Map" resolution (A/RES/80/297), arguing that correcting cartographic representation is a matter of cognitive justice — recognizing and contesting inherited colonial ways of seeing the world.

Key takeaways
  • 164 UN Member States adopted resolution A/RES/80/297, with only one voting against
  • The resolution was led by Togo on behalf of the African Group, building on an African Union campaign
  • The Equal Earth projection was developed in 2018 by researchers at Esri, US National Park Service, and Monash University
  • Togo's Foreign Minister Robert Dussey framed the issue as "cognitive justice" — access to geographical knowledge, dignity, and historical memory
  • The Mercator projection "midwifed a particular global socio-economic and political order" centered on Europe
  • The author argues that no perfectly neutral map exists; every projection involves choices about what to preserve

Will the UN Decision Change Our World Maps?

The UN General Assembly adopted a resolution with 164 votes in favor and one against, calling for world maps to use representations that more faithfully reflect the relative size of continents — favoring the Equal Earth projection over the colonial-era Mercator projection.

Key takeaways
  • The resolution was passed with 164 votes for and 1 against, presented by a coalition of African countries led by Togo
  • The Equal Earth projection, developed in 2018, preserves proportional area while accepting distortions elsewhere
  • Greenland appears similar in size to Africa on Mercator maps, but Africa is actually 14 times larger
  • Brazil appears the same size as Alaska on Mercator but is in reality five times larger
  • UQAM geography professor Rodolphe Gonzalès frames this as a "symbolic injustice, a geometric injustice between North and South"
  • Google Maps and other navigators predominantly use Mercator because it enables smooth zoom
2026-09-10 Sarah Boumedda (Le Devoir) Source article

Field Evaluation of Photogrammetric SLAM for Infrastructure Asset Mapping

A field evaluation at BCIT compares Looq AI's handheld photogrammetric mapping platform against Total Station and GNSS RTK survey methods for infrastructure asset mapping, finding that the system can support precision mapping when used with rigorous survey control protocols.

Key takeaways
  • Looq AI's Platform combines imagery, GNSS, and inertial sensing to produce georeferenced 3D data
  • Evaluation conducted on a 150m x 50m outdoor plaza at BCIT Burnaby campus with ~45-47 manhole/utility features
  • Reference framework established via Leica TS13 Robotic Total Station with closed traverse tied to BCIT geodetic network
  • Leica GS06 GNSS RTK receiver provided comparison via Leica SmartNet CORS network
  • In the no-control test, the Looq dataset exceeded the 50mm tolerance for GIS asset management
  • With external ground control alignment, accuracy improved significantly
  • Wet surface conditions from post-rain capture did not significantly affect geometry or detection accuracy

Satellite Navigators Concentrate Traffic on Few Roads, Reducing Environmental Benefits

A study published in Nature Communications shows that when adoption of navigation apps like Google Maps and TomTom exceeds 60–80%, traffic concentrates on few roads and environmental benefits disappear or reverse.

Key takeaways
  • Research by CNR-Isti, University of Pisa, and Scuola Normale Superiore simulated traffic in Florence, Milan, and Rome using GPS data cross-referenced with Google Maps, TomTom, Bing Maps, and Mapbox routing
  • Route diversity decreases up to 14% at full adoption, pushing vehicles toward major arteries and highways
  • With light traffic, navigators reduce CO2 emissions; with heavy traffic, benefits only hold below 60–80% adoption
  • Beyond that threshold, benefits "attenuate, vanish, or even reverse" — in some Rome scenarios, emissions actually increased
  • The study highlights how individual-level optimization algorithms can produce collectively harmful outcomes at scale
2026-09-09 Sky TG24 Source article

This Little-Known Google Maps Setting Saves Your Battery and Mobile Data

Google Maps' offline maps feature can save both battery and mobile data, but a hidden default setting silently updates downloaded maps over cellular data without user confirmation — here's how to fix it.

Key takeaways

  • Google Maps' offline maps feature allows pre-downloading detailed maps to navigate without a network connection
  • Once downloaded, the app no longer needs to constantly request mobile data to display streets and points of interest
  • A hidden default setting automatically updates offline maps over both Wi-Fi and cellular data without asking for confirmation
  • The update process runs in the background with no notification or visible indication
  • Disabling "Automatically update offline maps" and "Automatically download recommended maps" prevents unwanted data consumption
  • Restricting offline map updates to Wi-Fi only further protects mobile data allowances

Why the UN's New World Map Won't Change Google Maps Anytime Soon

The UN's adoption of the Equal Earth projection resolution won't change Google Maps because the app's tiling system depends on Mercator's angle-preserving properties, and the resolution is nonbinding.

  • The UN resolution passed with 164 votes in favour, 1 against (US), and 6 abstentions, but is nonbinding
  • France announced it will switch official maps from Mercator to Eckert IV projection
  • Google Maps uses a square-tile system since 2005 that requires Mercator's angle-preserving properties at all zoom levels
  • Equal Earth and Eckert IV preserve surface areas but sacrifice angular accuracy, making them incompatible with current tile-based mapping infrastructure
  • Togo plans to meet with Google, the African Union, and UNESCO within six months to discuss practical implementation

What Different World Maps Get Right — and What They Get Wrong

The BBC provides a comparative analysis of the world's most prominent map projections — Mercator, Equal Earth, and Peters — explaining the trade-offs between area accuracy, shape fidelity, and navigational utility.

Key takeaways
  • No flat map can perfectly represent a spherical Earth; every projection sacrifices something
  • Mercator preserves compass bearings but massively distorts area, making Africa look Greenland-sized
  • Equal Earth, adopted by the UN, preserves area accuracy but cannot be used for navigation
  • The Peters projection (1973) also preserves area but severely distorts shapes of landmasses
  • Critics argue Mercator's distortions have psychological effects, shaping how regions are perceived politically and economically
